entities.summary:
Erridupizir (Erridu-pizir) was a Gutian ruler in Sumer who called himself 'King of Guti, King of the Four Quarters' and was thought to be the 'king without a name' on the SKL. His reign was attested by a royal inscription at the archaeological site of Nippur. Imta succeeded Erridupizir after his death in 2300 BCE.



Erridupizir's significance lies in his role as a Gutian ruler in Sumer, where he marked a period of transition between the Sumerian and Akkadian periods. His inscription at Nippur provides valuable information about the politics and culture of the region during this time.




Erridupizir's legacy can be seen in the continued influence of the Gutian Empire on the region, and his inscription at Nippur remains an important source for historians studying the history of Sumer.




Imta's succession marked the beginning of a new era in Sumer, as the Akkadian Empire began to rise to power. Erridupizir's reign was a crucial period in the transition from the Sumerian to the Akkadian period, and his inscription at Nippur remains an important artifact for understanding this time period.




A striking statistic about Erridupizir is that he was one of the few Gutian rulers to be mentioned in the Epic of Gilgamesh, which provides valuable insight into the cultural and political landscape of the region during this time.
